p: Dani took the LSAT on Saturday, June twelfth, at a test center in the Tech Center, with Teo waiting outside in the truck.
He found the envelope in her prep book and sat with it all four hours: maybe he did it on the front, and on the back, who was the kid, with his own name under it.
When she came out he told her he was in their father's truck when it drove out of that lot.
Then he said it wasn't Pa. He was the one who hit the man.
Before the test, Ana lent her the 2010 opinion from her top drawer, with a small circled one in old pencil beside the jacket sentence.
Teo Ruiz. Thirty now. The one who was in the truck.
Ana Brennan. Still Dani's teacher, with the test behind them.
Luis Ruiz. He doesn't know yet what Teo said in the truck.
Bianca Medina. Lupe's mother, and Teo's partner.
Ingrid Solberg. The Denver pathologist reading the old autopsy.

In the truck he'd said that much and then couldn't say the rest of it. She waited. Two rows over a woman buckled a kid into a car seat and drove off, and somebody else pulled into the space, and her brother sat with both hands on the wheel of a truck that wasn't going anywhere. After a while he put it in gear. He drove her home on 25 with the radio off and the envelope on the dash, and at her curb he left the engine running.

Not today, he said. I'll tell you all of it. I can't today. She said okay. It was the one thing she could think of that wouldn't cost him anything. He waited at the curb until she had the front door open, the way their father used to wait when he dropped her at a friend's house, and then he went.

Monday, June 14, she told Ana at the desk on Federal, standing up, with her bag still on her shoulder. Teo was in the truck when it left the lot. Teo says he hit the man. That's all he's said. Ana didn't write any of it down. She looked out the window at the bus bench across the street for a while and then back at Dani. Then that's what you know, she said. When he tells you the rest, I want it the next morning. And you don't interview him. He's your brother. Let him tell it however he tells it.

Two Wednesdays went by. Her father called at seven both times and talked about the heat on the tier, and about Darnell, who'd finally passed the math part of his GED on the third try and cried, like her father said he would. The board sat on the kitchen table where it had sat since May. It was her move. He didn't ask for it, and she didn't tell him anything about the truck.
Wednesday, June 30. At 5:58 the phone lit up on the nightstand.
A text from Teo. you up

She was. She'd been up since four, listening to the sprinklers come on across the street. She wrote back yeah, and he wrote back that Bianca had looked it up and the scores came out at seven, and then nothing, and she pictured him sitting in the truck in his driveway with the phone on his knee.
At 7:01 the email came. She signed in at the kitchen table with her coffee going cold next to the laptop, and there it was. One sixty five.

It was about where her practice tests had said it would land, a point under the last three of them. She looked at it long enough to be sure it wasn't going to change, and then she got up and rinsed the cup out at the sink and set it upside down.
She texted Teo that it was good.
A text from Teo. lupe wants to know did you win
She told him to tell Lupe yes. Three minutes later he wrote again.
A text from Teo. saturday the 10th. after shes asleep. ill tell you

At nine, at the office, Joel came down the hall with his coffee and stopped at the end of her desk, and didn't say anything, and waited. She held her phone out. He read it off the screen and handed it back. The letter's still in my drawer, he said. It's still true. After September. I didn't ask when. He knocked twice on the desk and went on down the hall.
She'd said after once before, at twenty, about Ma. After had taken fourteen years.
That night at seven she gave her father the number on the step. He made her say it again, slower, and she did. He didn't ask what it meant, and she didn't tell him about the other text.

Saturday, July 10, at a quarter to nine, Bianca let her in under the carport. The string lights from March were still up, unplugged. He's been out in the truck every night since June, she said, low, at the door. I'll be in the back with my book. She's asleep. She sleeps like him. Nothing wakes her. Somebody had wiped down the stove and put the dish rack under the sink. Two glasses of water on the table. Down the hall Lupe's door was open about an inch. Her nightlight was a turtle.
Teo sat down across from her and put his hands flat on the table, like he was about to get up again. I'm going to go straight through, he said. Don't stop me, or I won't get back to it.

I begged him, Teo said. That's how it starts. Ma's on nights, the Rockies are in the Series for the first time ever, I'm ten. I begged him from Thursday on. Saturday he comes home from the plant and he goes, fine, get your shoes. A table in the back, by the hallway where the bathrooms were. Every time Pa went up to the bar he came back with a Sprite for Teo, and the first couple of times a beer for himself, and Teo kept count. Five Sprites, more than Ma let him have in a week. There was a big guy in a purple Rockies shirt who'd been on them since the third inning.

Last out, I've had like five Sprites, I run for the bathroom. There's a beer on the end of the bar and I hit it with my elbow, and it goes right down the front of the purple shirt guy. He grabs me here. Teo held his own arm above the elbow. And he shakes me. I'm ten, my feet are barely on the floor, and he's yelling down in my face, I still don't know what. Then Pa's there. Pa hit him first. I saw it. After that it's legs, all I can see is legs, and Ronnie's yelling for them to take it outside. Pa finds me by the back of my shirt and walks me out the back ahead of him. Nobody ever looked down.
He told it to the table. Every few sentences he looked down the hall at the crack in Lupe's door.

Out back he puts me in the truck and says stay, and the guy comes out after him and gets him on the tailgate. The flashlight from the plant was behind the seat. I hit him with it, one time. He touched his face. He let go and walked off holding his face, bleeding. I wiped my hands on Pa's sleeve. Then I'm crying for him. Papi, Papi.
Ten to eleven, by a stove clock across the street. Dani held her glass and didn't drink from it.

He gets me back in the truck and we go. Not home. He goes out Highway 2 and around the long way toward the highway and pulls into a gas station by the on ramp. It's a tire place now. He pumps gas with his sleeve pushed up so I won't look at it, and he comes back with a blue Gatorade for me. I didn't even want it. I held it the whole rest of the night in both hands. The clock over the register said 11:05. I'd never been up that late in my life. I looked right at it so I'd remember. And Pa gets his receipt and balls it up and puts it in the can by the pump.

Under ENOUGH on the envelope, in her own hand since December, it said somewhere else at 11:15. Her brother had read every line on that envelope in a parking lot in June, and he had no idea he'd just answered one of them.

Not for gas, she'd said to her father on the step in January. Straight home, mija. That was a man who'd stood at a pump by the interstate ten minutes before somebody hit Travis Hensley at that curb, with a piece of paper in his hand that had the time on it, and he'd put it in a trash can. A man who didn't do it, throwing away the one thing that said so.
Her brother was watching her. He'd seen something go across her face and didn't know what.
That receipt put Pa at a pump at 11:05, Teo. The camera over the pump had you.

Teo asks what camera. She tells him that a station with a register has a tape, and a receipt with the time on it is how anybody finds the right minute of the tape. Anybody who went looking for that night would have found a boy in the front seat holding a blue Gatorade in both hands. Teo says he never once thought about the time. He'd looked at the clock so he'd remember being up late. That's all it ever was to him.

She told him about the curb then, because nobody ever had. A quarter past eleven. A woman across the street at her kitchen window. A man in a red jacket and a ball cap who hit Travis Hensley with something and ran off on foot, and Travis going over backward against the curb. Teo listened with his jaw set.
He was bleeding all over, he said. You didn't see him. He was already going. Whoever that was, he was already going.
She didn't argue with him. He went on, because he'd said he would.

He goes the back way to Globeville, and in the middle of the bridge over the Platte he stops. Flashers on. He gets out with the flashlight. I'm watching him in the side mirror. Then he drops it over the rail. I didn't hear it go in. I looked it up once, how deep the Platte is there. Not very.
So by ten past eleven, give or take, the flashlight was in the Platte, and at a quarter past a man at the curb hit Travis Hensley with something.

Abuela's got the porch light on before we're up the steps. She doesn't ask anything. She takes me to the sink and washes my hands with the dish soap, hot as it goes, and dries them one finger at a time with a dish towel, and gives me a cookie. I didn't eat it. Pa's in the hall with her talking Spanish, low. I heard enough of it. Say he was here since supper. Say he was here all night.

And she did, he said. To Ma. To you. To the priest, probably. To everybody, till she died. He turned his glass a quarter turn on the table. She never told a lie in her life, Dani. When I was six she made me walk a candy bar back to the store and say sorry to the man. She went to Mass every morning, and she lied for me for eight years. You know what that means. She knew what I did.
All she ever lied about was where you were, Teo. A boy in that lot was enough for her.

Teo says that isn't the same thing. She says it's the whole difference. Abuela's lie was about a place. It didn't need her to know anything about the lot except that a ten year old had been in it, and she'd washed what was on his hands without once asking what it was. He sits with that. He doesn't say she's right, and he doesn't say she's wrong.

Sunday Abuela drove him home after lunch. Dani was already there. She'd come home from the sleepover in Thornton at eight that morning, and she'd been down to the basement once already and seen the jacket in the washer, and come back up and said nothing to anybody, because Ma was asleep from her shift, and the only other person up was Pa, at the kitchen table, and it was his jacket.

A guy in a tan coat comes at three, Teo said. You take him down the basement. I'm on the top step in my socks. You've got your back to the stairs the whole time. I hear you tell him Ma does the wash on Mondays. Then he comes back up past me with Pa's jacket in a paper bag, and he says excuse me, son. Like I'm in his way.
She'd stayed down by the washer after, she remembered that, a long while, with her hand on the lid. She'd never known he was on the stairs. Fifteen, and right there, and she'd never once seen him.

Monday Pa was gone. In June, while she was in Brighton telling a jury about the jacket, Teo stayed with Abuela, and nobody told him anything, and he didn't ask. He worked it out himself from the news on TV and from Ma crying in the car and from what he knew, which was more than anybody in that courtroom.
Then Ma. The viewing, the hour they gave Pa, the two officers at the back. She knew where she'd been standing. Six feet off, with their aunt's purse on her arm.
He said it now, in their father's voice, or near it. 'You were at Abuela's, mijo. You were always at Abuela's.'
Nothing else. Over their mother, with his hand on Teo's shoulder.

Teo was at Abuela's. She'd thought it in Consuelo's kitchen in February, at ten to eleven by the stove clock, like something she knew. Everybody knew where Teo was. Pa had seen to that, and at the casket he'd seen to Teo.
So that's it, he said. I hit a man in the head with a steel flashlight, and he died that night, and Pa's done every day of it since. That's what I've got.

She'd read the report on June 11, the night before the test, at about this hour, and gotten every answer in the margin right. She had the words right there, and she nearly said them, and didn't. Not until she knew they fit what he'd done.
Where did it hit him, Teo? Show me where on his face it caught him.
Over the eye, he says. The left one. He doesn't have to think about it. If he'd said the back of the head, she'd have had nothing to tell him. He hadn't.

Somewhere in the telling his hand had gone up to his own face, to the left side above the eyebrow, two fingers, like you'd touch a bruise to see if it was still there. She didn't think he knew he did it. He'd probably been doing it since he was ten.
She could see the page. She'd read it like Ana told her to, like a passage, and it was all still there.

What she remembered of the report, word for word. Laceration, two and a half centimeters, above the left eyebrow. Superficial. Does not reach the bone. Depressed fracture of the back of the skull. The fatal injury is the depressed fracture at the back of the skull. The laceration above the left eyebrow is a separate, superficial injury and is non-contributory.
Ana's rule for this kind was always the same. Use the page's words, not yours, and put them on what he did.

She puts the page's words on his swing. A cut above the left eye, superficial, separate from what killed him. It was a real cut. It bled, and cuts there do. It had nothing to do with how the night ended.
She kept her voice down, for Lupe. You cut his eyebrow.

He looked at her. It's in the autopsy. Ana gave it to me in June. There's two injuries on page one, Teo. The back of his head is what killed him. Over his eye, it didn't even get to the bone. The doctor's got a word for that. She said it like it was typed. Non-contributory.

That's a piece of paper, he said, after a while. I was there. He was bleeding all down his shirt. A cut there bleeds like that. And at four minutes after eleven he was on the phone to his sister. Talking. Twenty minutes after you. People talk when they're dying. You see it on TV.
He wasn't going to put it down in one night, she could see that. He'd been carrying it since he was ten.

But there were two things on the table now, his and the report's, and if both of them were right, then one thing about that night couldn't be. She knew which one. She had to say it so he'd hear it as a fact, and not as his sister being kind.
Then it can't be true that your swing killed him. One swing, there, and he walked off.

Teo says she doesn't know that. She says she knows what the report says and what he just told her, and those two can't both be right if his swing is what killed Travis Hensley. He gets up and goes down the hall and stands in Lupe's door a while with his back to the kitchen. When he comes back he says, I don't know, and sits down, and she lets that be enough for one night.
She drove home at midnight down 104th with the windows open and nothing on. The envelope was in the prep book on the passenger seat, and she didn't take it out till she was home.

At the kitchen table she took the envelope out after all. Under ENOUGH, small, in pencil, she wrote 11:05, A PUMP BY THE ON RAMP. She left the top line where it was, in her own capitals from December. A pencil hadn't put it there, and a pencil wasn't going to take it off.
She didn't need Gene's notebook for the rest. She had his voice. Monday night, six hours in a room, and her father had asked him one thing. Was anybody else hurt?
He'd told her at the end, sitting on the stool by the covered car, and said he'd quit thinking about it.

Strange thing for a guilty man to ask, Gene had said. Strange for an innocent one too. In January she'd sat in his drive with the engine running and counted her family. Her in Thornton. Mom at work. Teo with Abuela. There wasn't anybody else.
There was. He'd been in the lot.
So her father hadn't done it, and the one thing he'd asked the man who arrested him was the thing Gene couldn't make fit. She sat with it under the lamp and tried to make it fit.

Anybody else. A guilty man knows who got hurt, because he did it. A man who was never there doesn't think anybody was. Her father had watched Travis go off across the lot holding his face, and driven away, and on Monday night somebody told him the man was dead at a curb. He was asking what happened after he left. Gene had been right that it was strange. It was only strange for the man Gene thought he had.

Resolve the paradox. Gene's puzzle was a question that fit neither a guilty man nor an innocent one. It fits a third kind of man: one who saw the fight begin, saw Travis walk off hurt, and left before the end. He knows there was violence, and he doesn't know who else it reached.

At one in the morning she had the report out of the folder and flat on the table under the lamp, the copy Ana gave her in June, eight pages stapled at the corner. She read the last paragraph again, the 2007 doctor's. Then the page with the two injuries on it, one above the other.

Teo needed an order. A blow, then a man walking off, then a curb. The State had needed an order too, the other way around. She wanted to know how much of anybody's order was on this page, and how much she'd be bringing to it.

And the cuff. The blood on it was the third thing the court had leaned on in 2010, after the jacket and the fight. Some of what was on that sleeve had come off a ten year old's hands before ten to eleven, twenty five minutes before anybody was at the curb.
Line two on Ana's board said the attack or the bar. Some of it was neither.

Separate, and that's all. The page doesn't keep time. She turns her card over and writes the times down from where they came from. Ten to eleven, the boy crying, by Consuelo's stove. 11:04, the call to Shannon. 11:05, the register over Teo's Gatorade. 11:15, Consuelo at her window again. The report isn't in any of them. Every clock that night belonged to somebody else, and the one Teo read, he read at ten.

Inference. The report calls the injuries separate, which means two distinct injuries, not one. It says nothing about when either happened, so you can't infer how much time passed between them. The order has to come from the witnesses.

Sunday, July 11. She found the corner on the map on her phone at seven, before coffee. Teo had said by the on ramp, and there was only one on ramp it could be. It was a tire shop now, like he'd said. Four miles from where the Night Owl had stood.
When he tells you the rest, I want it the next morning. It was the next morning, and a Sunday. Monday at seven, then, before her bus. That gave her a day to try to break it first.

She wrote it on a card first, as Ana would have made her. PA AT A PUMP FOUR MILES OFF AT 11:05. SO PA WASN'T THE MAN AT THE CURB AT 11:15. If she walked in on Federal with an argument, it had better be one she'd already tried to break.

She maps it back the other way. Eleven minutes at night, the phone says, if every light goes green. Ten minutes on one clock and eleven on the road, and nobody ever checked the station's clock against Consuelo's. Too close to carry it alone, and she's glad she found that out before Ana did. Then the rest of it, which only Teo had. The pump, then the bridge, then Abuela's porch, and Teo in the cab for all of it. The man at the curb ran off on foot. She puts it on the card, and next to it, small, TEO'S WORD. Ana would ask. At nine she texts Teo that she has to tell Ana tomorrow, and he writes back i know. Monday at seven she tells Ana all of it, in order, standing at the desk.

Evaluate the argument. The argument moves from four miles away at 11:05 to not at the curb at 11:15. Ask whether he could get back in time. If he could, the pump doesn't settle it and you need more. If he couldn't, the argument holds. Either answer changes it.
On Monday Ana had written every line of it down in pencil, read it back to her, and changed nothing. Friday, July 16, at twenty to seven in the evening, Bianca texted.
A text from Bianca. he went to anas this morning. didnt tell me till tonight. he says tell dani its done

He'd gone up the stairs on Federal by himself. Ana told it to her plainly on Tuesday, the way she told everything. He'd sat in the chair and asked what it would take for them to have his DNA. She'd told him she was his father's lawyer and not his, that anything he said to her she might have to use, and that he should talk to a lawyer of his own first. She wrote him a name. He said he'd heard her. Then Ana called Meredith, because the order said the parties would confer on the testing, and conferring was what they did. At three that afternoon an investigator from the district attorney's office swabbed the inside of his cheek at Ana's desk and sealed it in front of both of them, and they both signed the form.
Teo asked one thing before he went back to work. If it's me under there, it says so? It says whatever's there, Ana told him, and he said okay.
So he'd done it still thinking it might be him. Dani hadn't been in the room for any of it.

Tuesday, July 20, she brought the opinion back. The coffee ring on the back, the small circled 1 in the margin of page eleven beside the one sentence. Ana took it without looking at it. She opened the top drawer and laid it in face down and shut the drawer. Dani didn't ask about the 1. She'd decided that on the bus.

She wrote, Ana said, and put a single page on the desk, face up, with a paper clip at the top. Dr. Solberg. It came yesterday. Before you read it, read 2007 one more time. Not what it says. How it talks. She slid the old report over beside the letter, open to its last paragraph.
Plain and certain. It names each injury, then which one killed him.

Sure about what it looked at, Ana says. And not one word past it. No who, no when, no how sorry anybody is. She taps the words fatal injury. That's somebody who's done a lot of these and doesn't need anybody to like the report.
Author's attitude. The report states its findings without qualification and ranks the injuries, one fatal and one non-contributory. That's confident and neutral, and it never goes past the body.

Ingrid Solberg, M.D., forensic pathology, Denver. Letter to Ana Brennan, Monday, July 19, 2027. You asked me to review the 2007 report of autopsy on Travis Hensley and to tell you what its findings establish. I have read the report, the fourteen photographs taken at autopsy, and the hospital record. I agree with the original pathologist on the cause of death. The fatal injury is the depressed fracture at the back of the skull. Its features are consistent with a blow from an object or with the back of the head striking a hard edge, such as a curb. The findings alone don't tell me which. The laceration above the left eyebrow is superficial and does not involve the bone. A wound there bleeds freely and can look far worse than it is. It would not have caused death, and in my opinion it did not contribute to it, which is what the original report means by non-contributory. I can't tell from the record which injury came first or how much time separated them. He lived for some hours after he reached the hospital, so the bruising doesn't settle the order. I have kept this opinion to what the record shows. For anything more than that you'll need a witness. The body won't tell you.
Dani read it twice. Ana waited, and drank her coffee, and let her.
Five paragraphs, and in the last one she tells you how she wrote the other four, Ana said. What's the rule she's working by?

Say what the findings show and where they stop, Dani says. That's the whole letter, Ana says. She agrees where she can, she won't guess at the order, and she tells me so in writing. A judge will believe every word of it for exactly that reason. She puts the letter in the folder, on top.

Principle. Solberg states it herself: she has kept her opinion to what the record shows. She agrees where the findings support it, declines to say which injury came first, and says where the evidence stops.
Ana took a card out of the box and wrote on it in capitals, slowly, the way she wrote the State's arguments. THE FRACTURE KILLED HIM. THE CUT DIDN'T. TEO MADE THE CUT. SO TEO DIDN'T KILL HIM.
Your brother's going to read this someday, one way or another, she said. So it had better be true all the way down. What do you add to it to make the last line have to follow?

The cut over his eye was the only harm Teo ever did him, she says. That's the piece, Ana says. She writes it in small between lines three and four. And it isn't a medical question. Solberg can't give it to you. A cut doesn't say whether the man fell down afterward. She taps the card. Your brother can say he walked off. And a phone call at 11:04 says he was still talking twenty minutes later.

Sufficient assumption. The premises say the cut wasn't fatal and Teo made it. To guarantee he didn't kill Travis, you need the cut to be everything his swing did: no fall it caused, no second injury. Add that, and the conclusion has to follow.

Ana had called her father on Friday afternoon, after the swab, a legal call, the little room with the phone on the wall. She'd told him all of it, she said, because he was her client and it was his case, and because otherwise he'd hear it from somebody worse.
Wednesday, July 21, seven. Her step. The recording, and then him, and no hello. Brennan called.

She waited. Behind him somebody was yelling about a card game. In June he'd asked her what she and her brother talked about, all that way in a truck, and she'd told him nothing, same as always. She heard the question now for what it had been.
He was ten years old, he said. Ten.

Ten years he won't come up here, he said. Not a card at Christmas. Not once on the phone. And now he walks up Brennan's stairs by himself and gives them his spit in a tube. A breath. He doesn't testify. I told Brennan and I'm telling you. He doesn't get up there.
Ten years of nothing and then that. He wanted somebody to tell him how it was the same boy.
At Ma's casket you told him where he'd been, Pa. He kept it ten years. Then he told me.

He doesn't say anything right away. Then: He told you that. He told me all of it, Pa. Not on this phone, mija. She hears him breathe out. Ten years of a boy keeping what his father told him over his mother's casket, and one Friday on Federal when he quit keeping it. One answer covers both. He doesn't testify, her father says again, quieter.

He didn't say it again on the next Wednesday call, or the one after that, but he didn't take it back either. He talked about the heat. Rudy had a hearing date on his new expert. Somebody on the tier had gotten a picture of a puppy from home and passed it around until it came apart at the fold. The board sat on her kitchen table with her move still in it.
Ana had nothing from the lab. When they get to it, she said, every time Dani asked, which was every time.
Wednesday, August 18, at ten after four, her phone buzzed on her desk at the office with Ana's name on it, and she took it out to the stairwell.
Your brother was here at noon, Ana said. On his lunch, with the grease still on his hands. He sat down and said he'll testify.
Dani sat down on the step. Two floors down somebody let the street door bang shut.

I told him his father said no. He said his father doesn't get a vote on what he says to a judge. A pause. Then he asked me to call you. He said if he told you himself, you'd start helping him with it, and after that he'd never know which part was his.

What did you tell him? That I'd call you. Ana's chair creaked. Your father's my client. Your brother isn't. I'll work out what that means, and I'm not going to work it out on the phone with you sitting in a stairwell. Go back to your desk.

She went back to her desk. She did the rest of the afternoon's work and some of tomorrow's, and took the 5:40 bus home with the prep book shut on her lap. There wasn't any test in it anymore. She kept carrying it anyway.
At ten to seven she stood at the kitchen table over the board. It had been her move since May. She'd looked at it every night for three months and never picked anything up.
She moved her knight up to the middle of the board. He'd have to answer it or leave it there, and either way it was his turn.

At seven she was on the step with the phone, and it rang. Recording, then him, and she gave him the move before he could ask for it, knight to the middle, the square by number like he'd taught her at eight on the back of a cereal box.
Then she waited while he found it on his own board, and listened to the tier behind him, a TV, somebody at the next phone arguing about money, a door. There she is, he said.
